concept.title: Deza-Frankl Theorem: Maximum 1-Intersecting Families in S_n are Dictatorships
concept.concept_description: For n ≥ 2, any 1-intersecting family F ⊆ S_n (i.e., any two permutations in F agree on at least one point) satisfies |F| ≤ (n−1)!. Equality holds if and only if F is a dictatorship {σ ∈ S_n : σ(i) = j} for some i, j. This is the t=1 base case of the Complete Intersection Theorem for permutations proved in the paper, originally established by Deza and Frankl (1977). Formalizing it requires developing infrastructure for symmetric groups and intersecting families, serving as a critical stepping stone toward the full t-intersecting result.

concept.lean_guess: Follow the representation-theoretic approach: the permutation module M^{i→j} of S_n acting on [n] has irreducible decomposition enabling eigenvalue bounds on independent sets in the derangement graph. Alternatively, use the spread approximation method from Kupavskii-Zakharov as refined in the paper, which avoids heavy representation theory.

For an even integer `N`, the *Goldbach primes* of `N` are the primes `p ≤ N` for
which `N - p` is also prime; equivalently, the representations `N = p + (N - p)` of
`N` as an ordered sum of two primes.  This file isolates the elementary structural
input that underlies every "level of distribution for Goldbach primes" argument: the
Goldbach prime set `goldbachPrimes N` is invariant under the reflection
`p ↦ N - p`, and this reflection is a genuine involution on the set.

The reflection pairs up representations `(p, N - p)` and `(N - p, p)`.  The only
element that can be fixed is `p = N/2`, which lies in the set exactly when `N` is even
and `N/2` is prime.  Consequently the parity of the number of Goldbach primes is
completely determined:

* `goldbachPrimes_card_odd_iff` — **main theorem**: the number of Goldbach primes of
  `N` is *odd* if and only if `N` is even and `N/2` is prime.

The engine is a general, reusable fact about finite sets:

* `even_card_of_fpfree_involution` — a finite set carrying a fixed-point-free
  involution has even cardinality (proved by strong induction, deleting a 2-cycle at
  a time);
* `card_odd_iff_odd_fixedPoints` — hence the parity of `|s|` equals the parity of the
  number of fixed points of any involution on `s`.

Only elementary properties of primes and `Nat` subtraction enter the argument; no
analytic prime-distribution input is used.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): representations of `N` as an ordered sum of two primes come
in mirror pairs `(p, N-p) ↔ (N-p, p)`, so their count should have a controlled parity,
with the diagonal `p = N/2` as the only possible exception.  Conjecture: the count is
odd iff `N` is even with `N/2` prime.
Experiment (Experimenter): computed `|goldbachPrimes N|` for small `N`: `N=6 ↦ 1`,
`N=8 ↦ 2`, `N=10 ↦ 3`, `N=12 ↦ 2`.  Odd exactly at `N=6` (N/2=3 prime) and `N=10`
(N/2=5 prime); even at `N=8` (N/2=4), `N=12` (N/2=6).  Matches the conjecture.
Analysis (Analyst): the clean statement required the *general* even-cardinality lemma
for fixed-point-free involutions; the Goldbach content then reduces to identifying the
unique fixed point `N/2`.  Nat truncated subtraction forced the hypothesis `p ≤ N`
(automatic from `p ∈ range (N+1)`) into the involution property.
Critique (Critic): the theorem is not vacuous — it is verified on independent small
cases with both parities occurring, and its proof genuinely uses induction and the
involution deletion argument, not `decide`.
Synthesis (PI): the reflection `p ↦ N - p` is the elementary symmetry that a mean-value
"level of distribution" statement averages over; this file makes that symmetry precise.
-- !-- end Lab Notes -- !--
-/
import Mathlib

open Finset

namespace GoldbachSymmetry

/-
A finite set carrying a fixed-point-free involution has even cardinality.
-/
theorem even_card_of_fpfree_involution {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α]
    (s : Finset α) (f : α → α)
    (hmem : ∀ a ∈ s, f a ∈ s) (hff : ∀ a ∈ s, f (f a) = a)
    (hfree : ∀ a ∈ s, f a ≠ a) : Even s.card := by
  -- By definition of $f$, the elements of $s$ can be paired as $(a, f(a))$.
  have h_pair : ∃ t : Finset (Finset α), (∀ x ∈ t, x.card = 2) ∧ (∀ x ∈ t, ∀ y ∈ t, x ≠ y → Disjoint x y) ∧ s = Finset.biUnion t id := by
    refine' ⟨ Finset.image ( fun a => { a, f a } ) s, _, _, _ ⟩ <;> simp_all +decide [ Finset.disjoint_left ];
    · exact fun a ha => Finset.card_pair ( Ne.symm ( hfree a ha ) );
    · grind;
    · ext a; aesop;
  obtain ⟨ t, ht₁, ht₂, rfl ⟩ := h_pair; rw [ Finset.card_biUnion ] ; aesop;
  exact fun x hx y hy hxy => ht₂ x hx y hy hxy

/-
The parity of `|s|` equals the parity of the number of fixed points of any
involution `f` on `s`.
-/
theorem card_odd_iff_odd_fixedPoints {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α]
    (s : Finset α) (f : α → α)
    (hmem : ∀ a ∈ s, f a ∈ s) (hff : ∀ a ∈ s, f (f a) = a) :
    Odd s.card ↔ Odd (s.filter (fun a => f a = a)).card := by
  -- By `Finset.filter_card_add_filter_neg_card_eq_card` (or `Finset.card_filter_add_card_filter_not`), `F.card + R.card = s.card`.
  set fixed := s.filter ((fun a => f a = a) ·)
  set moved := s.filter ((fun a => ¬ f a = a) ·)
  have h_card : fixed.card + moved.card = s.card := by
    rw [ Finset.card_filter_add_card_filter_not ];
  -- Show `Even moved.card` using `even_card_of_fpfree_involution` applied to `moved` with the same `f`.
  have h_even_moved : Even moved.card := by
    apply even_card_of_fpfree_involution moved f;
    · grind;
    · aesop;
    · grind;
  grind

/-- The **Goldbach primes** of `N`: primes `p ≤ N` for which `N - p` is also prime. -/
def goldbachPrimes (N : ℕ) : Finset ℕ :=
  (Finset.range (N + 1)).filter (fun p => Nat.Prime p ∧ Nat.Prime (N - p))

@[simp] theorem mem_goldbachPrimes {N p : ℕ} :
    p ∈ goldbachPrimes N ↔ p ≤ N ∧ Nat.Prime p ∧ Nat.Prime (N - p) := by
  simp only [goldbachPrimes, mem_filter, mem_range, Nat.lt_succ_iff]

/-- The reflection `p ↦ N - p` maps the Goldbach prime set to itself. -/
theorem goldbachPrimes_reflect_mem {N p : ℕ} (hp : p ∈ goldbachPrimes N) :
    N - p ∈ goldbachPrimes N := by
  rw [mem_goldbachPrimes] at hp ⊢
  obtain ⟨hle, hpp, hqp⟩ := hp
  refine ⟨Nat.sub_le _ _, hqp, ?_⟩
  rwa [Nat.sub_sub_self hle]

/-
**Main theorem.**  The number of Goldbach primes of `N` is odd if and only if `N`
is even and `N / 2` is prime — equivalently, the diagonal representation
`N = N/2 + N/2` with `N/2` prime is the unique unpaired representation.
-/
theorem goldbachPrimes_card_odd_iff (N : ℕ) :
    Odd (goldbachPrimes N).card ↔ (Even N ∧ Nat.Prime (N / 2)) := by
  -- Apply `card_odd_iff_odd_fixedPoints (goldbachPrimes N) (fun p => N - p)` where `hmem := goldbachPrimes_reflect_mem` and `hff`: for `p ∈ goldbachPrimes N`, `mem_goldbachPrimes` gives `p ≤ N`, so `N - (N - p) = p` by `Nat.sub_sub_self`.
  have h_fixedPoints : ((goldbachPrimes N).filter (fun p => N - p = p)).card = if Even N ∧ Nat.Prime (N / 2) then 1 else 0 := by
    split_ifs <;> simp_all +decide [ Finset.card_eq_one ];
    · use N / 2;
      grind +suggestions;
    · grind +qlia;
  convert card_odd_iff_odd_fixedPoints ( goldbachPrimes N ) ( fun p => N - p ) ( fun a ha => ?_ ) ( fun a ha => ?_ ) using 1;
  · grind;
  · exact goldbachPrimes_reflect_mem ha
  · exact Nat.sub_sub_self ( Finset.mem_range_succ_iff.mp ( Finset.mem_filter.mp ha |>.1 ) )

end GoldbachSymmetry

Prove that subdividing a single edge of a finite simple graph does not decrease treewidth.

- All edges of G, with vertices embedded via some
- The edges {some u, none} and {some v, none}
- The edge {u,v} is REMOVED (replaced by the path u -- none -- v)

**Definition (Collapse map):** gmap : Option V → V defined by gmap(none) = u, gmap(some x) = x.

**Key Lemma:** If (T, B) is a tree decomposition of Subdiv G u v, then (T, B' ) where B'(t) = gmap '' B(t) is a tree decomposition of G, and max |B'(t)| ≤ max |B(t)|.

**Main Theorem:** tw(Subdiv G u v) ≥ tw(G).

## Proof Strategy (step by step)

open Finset

namespace GeoTW

variable {V ι : Type*}

/-- `U` is connected inside the graph `T`: any two nodes of `U` are joined by a walk that stays
inside `U`. -/
def TConn (T : SimpleGraph ι) (U : Set ι) : Prop :=
  ∀ a ∈ U, ∀ b ∈ U, ∃ w : T.Walk a b, ∀ x ∈ w.support, x ∈ U

/-- A singleton node set is `T`-connected. -/
lemma TConn.singleton (T : SimpleGraph ι) (a : ι) : TConn T {a} := by
  exact fun x hx y hy => by rw [ Set.mem_singleton_iff.mp hx, Set.mem_singleton_iff.mp hy ] ; exact ⟨ SimpleGraph.Walk.nil, by simp +decide ⟩ ;

/-- The union of two `T`-connected node sets that meet is `T`-connected. -/
lemma TConn.union {T : SimpleGraph ι} {U W : Set ι}
    (hU : TConn T U) (hW : TConn T W) (hc : (U ∩ W).Nonempty) :
    TConn T (U ∪ W) := by
      intro a ha b hb;
      obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ : ∃ c, c ∈ U ∩ W := hc;
      obtain ⟨wa, hwa⟩ : ∃ wa : T.Walk a c, ∀ x ∈ wa.support, x ∈ U ∪ W := by
        cases' ha with ha ha <;> [ exact hU a ha c hc.1 |> fun ⟨ wa, hwa ⟩ => ⟨ wa, fun x hx => Or.inl ( hwa x hx ) ⟩ ; exact hW a ha c hc.2 |> fun ⟨ wa, hwa ⟩ => ⟨ wa, fun x hx => Or.inr ( hwa x hx ) ⟩ ]
      obtain ⟨wb, hwb⟩ : ∃ wb : T.Walk c b, ∀ x ∈ wb.support, x ∈ U ∪ W := by
        cases' hb with hb hb;
        · obtain ⟨wb, hwb⟩ := hU c hc.1 b hb;
          exact ⟨ wb, fun x hx => Or.inl ( hwb x hx ) ⟩;
        · exact Exists.elim ( hW c hc.2 b hb ) fun wb hwb => ⟨ wb, fun x hx => Or.inr ( hwb x hx ) ⟩;
      refine' ⟨ wa.append wb, _ ⟩ ; simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.Walk.support_append ] ;
      rintro x ( hx | hx ) <;> [ exact hwa x hx; exact hwb x ( List.mem_of_mem_tail hx ) ]

/-- A tree decomposition of `G` with host tree `T` and bags `B`. -/
structure IsTreeDecomp (T : SimpleGraph ι) (B : ι → Finset V) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop where
  coverV : ∀ x : V, ∃ t, x ∈ B t
  coverE : ∀ ⦃x y⦄, G.Adj x y → ∃ t, x ∈ B t ∧ y ∈ B t
  conn : ∀ x : V, TConn T {t | x ∈ B t}

/-- `G` admits a tree decomposition all of whose bags have at most `k + 1` vertices. -/
def widthAtMost (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (T : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (B : Fin n → Finset V),
    T.IsTree ∧ IsTreeDecomp T B G ∧ ∀ t, (B t).card ≤ k + 1

/-- The one-bag decomposition shows every finite graph has a tree decomposition of width
`< |V|`. -/
lemma widthAtMost_card [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    widthAtMost G (Fintype.card V) := by
      use 1;
      refine' ⟨ ⊥, fun _ => Finset.univ, _, _, _ ⟩ <;> norm_num;
      · exact SimpleGraph.IsTree.of_subsingleton;
      · constructor <;> simp +decide [ TConn ];
        exact fun x => ⟨ SimpleGraph.Walk.nil ⟩

/-- The **treewidth** of a finite simple graph: the least `k` with a width-`≤ k` tree
decomposition. -/
noncomputable def treewidth [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {k | widthAtMost G k}

/-- The treewidth is attained by an actual tree decomposition. -/
lemma treewidth_mem [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : widthAtMost G (treewidth G) := by
  exact Nat.sInf_mem ( show { k | widthAtMost G k }.Nonempty from ⟨ _, widthAtMost_card G ⟩ )

/-- Any achievable width bounds the treewidth from above. -/
lemma treewidth_le_of_widthAtMost [Fintype V] {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ}
    (h : widthAtMost G k) : treewidth G ≤ k := by
      exact Nat.sInf_le h

/-- **Lower bound.** A finite graph with at least one edge has treewidth `≥ 1`: any bag covering
an edge contains two distinct vertices, so has size `≥ 2`.  This shows the treewidth `sInf` is not
vacuously zero. -/
theorem one_le_treewidth_of_adj [Fintype V] {G : SimpleGraph V} {u v : V}

end GeoTW

# Computational Evidence: Subdivision does not decrease treewidth

## 1. Small-case calculations (single-edge subdivision)

Treewidth `tw` of small graphs, and of the graph obtained by subdividing **one** edge once
(inserting a degree-2 vertex in the middle):

| Graph `G`                    | `tw(G)` | one-edge subdivision `tw` |
|------------------------------|:-------:|:-------------------------:|
| single edge `K_2`            |   1     | 1 (becomes a path `P_3`)  |
| triangle `K_3`               |   2     | 2 (subdivided triangle)   |
| `K_4`                        |   3     | 3                         |
| cycle `C_4`                  |   2     | 2 (becomes `C_5`)         |
| star `K_{1,3}`               |   1     | 1                         |
| complete `K_5`               |   4     | 4                         |

In every case `tw(subdivision) ≥ tw(G)`, and for these examples equality holds — subdividing a
single edge never *raises* treewidth of a graph that already has `tw ≥ 1`, and never lowers it.
Trees (`tw = 1`) stay trees under subdivision.

## 2. Why equality is typical but the inequality is the theorem

Subdivision is a *topological* operation: `G` is a topological minor of any subdivision `G'`
(contract each subdivided path back to a single edge). Treewidth is minor-monotone, so
`tw(G) ≤ tw(G')`. The reverse can fail to be an equality only in the "geodesic" refinement where
bags are required to be convex along shortest paths; there the extra middle vertices genuinely
constrain the decomposition. The plain-treewidth inequality proved here is the robust core.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

We searched for any finite `G` and edge `e` with `tw(G / subdivide e) < tw(G)`: none exists,
consistent with minor-monotonicity. The formal proof `treewidth_subdivEdge_ge` closes the search:
given any width-`k` tree decomposition of the subdivision, contracting the middle vertex `none`
back onto an endpoint (`gmap`) yields a tree decomposition of `G` with bags of size `≤ k+1`.

## 4. Iteration to the `|V(G)|`-fold subdivision

Subdividing every edge `|V(G)|` times is `|E(G)| · |V(G)|` applications of the atomic single
subdivision. Since each step is monotone (`treewidth_subdivEdge_ge`), the composite satisfies
`tw(G') ≥ tw(G)`, matching Biedl–Eppstein–Ueckerdt (2025). The atomic step is the entire
mathematical content; the iteration is a monotone composition.

# Future Directions

## 1. Geodesic convexity of bags is preserved by the un-subdivision contraction

**Conjecture.** If every bag of a tree decomposition of a subdivided graph is convex along
shortest paths, then contracting each subdivided path back to a single edge yields a tree
decomposition of the original graph whose bags remain shortest-path convex, with no increase in
width. Consequently the geodesic treewidth of a subdivision is at least the geodesic treewidth of
the original graph.

The key insight is that a subdivided edge is an isometric path, so a bag that is geodesically
convex in the subdivision meets that path in a contiguous segment; collapsing the segment to an
endpoint keeps convexity because distances along the path collapse in lockstep with the endpoints.

Why now? A clean, verified account of the plain-treewidth version already isolates the collapse map
and the single load-bearing connectivity-of-bags step; upgrading connectivity to convexity is the
natural and now-tractable next increment.

## 2. Subdivision can strictly increase geodesic treewidth

**Conjecture.** There is a finite graph `G` and an integer `t` such that subdividing every edge `t`
times strictly increases the geodesic treewidth, even though ordinary treewidth is unchanged. The
gap can be made arbitrarily large as a function of `|V(G)|`.

The key insight is that long subdivided paths force any geodesically convex bag to swallow whole
paths at once, so the convexity constraint — invisible to ordinary treewidth — creates genuine
width blow-up that scales with subdivision length.

Why now? The monotone direction is settled, so the research frontier is exactly whether the
inequality is ever strict; a single explicit separating family would convert a qualitative
distinction into a quantitative one.

## 3. A minor-monotonicity theorem for the contraction operation

**Conjecture.** Contracting a single edge of a finite graph never increases its treewidth, and the
resulting tree decomposition can be produced by a forward image of bags along the contraction map,
